hints: Look closely at Fig. 3.1 and find any carbon atom that is bonded to four single bonds and check if all four attached groups are different.
Recall which type of stereoisomerism arises when a molecule contains a single chiral centre and can exist as non-superimposable mirror images.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral carbon in T**
Draw out T in your mind: $(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_2CH_2CH(CH_3)CH_2CHO$. Focus on the carbon carrying the single methyl branch, $CH(CH_3)$. Its four bonds go to $H$, to $CH_3$, to $CH_2CHO$ on the right, and to $CH_2CH_2CH=C(CH_3)_2$ on the left. All four are different, so this is a chiral centre.

Link chirality to optical isomerism**
A molecule with one chiral centre can exist as two non-superimposable mirror images. These mirror images rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions. That pair is called optical isomers, so T shows optical isomerism.

Final answer: Optical isomerism.
One carbon atom in T is chiral as it is bonded to four different atoms / groups.

hints: Remember that hot concentrated acidified $KMnO_4$ both cleaves the $C=C$ double bond completely and oxidises the $-CHO$ group to $-COOH$.
Split T at the $C=C$ bond: the $(CH_3)_2C=$ end becomes a small ketone, while the rest of the chain plus the oxidised aldehyde becomes a dicarboxylic acid.
walkthrough:
Break the alkene apart**
Hot concentrated $KMnO_4$ cuts right through the $C=C$ bond. Think of $(CH_3)_2C=CH-$ as two pieces. The left piece $(CH_3)_2C=$ has no H to oxidise further, so it stops as the ketone $(CH_3)_2CO$, propanone.

Oxidise the two new ends**
The right piece $-CH=$ becomes $-COOH$ after cleavage. At the other end of the same molecule the aldehyde $-CHO$ is also oxidised to $-COOH$ under these vigorous conditions. Joining them gives $HOOC-CH_2-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-COOH$, which is 3-methylhexanedioic acid.

Final answer: Organic product 1: propanone, $(CH_3)_2CO$.
Organic product 2: 3-methylhexanedioic acid, $HOOC(CH_2)_2CH(CH_3)CH_2COOH$.

hints: Compare T and S and notice that only the $-CHO$ group changes to $-CH_2OH$ while the $C=C$ bond is unchanged, so a selective reducing agent is needed.
walkthrough:
Choose a gentle hydride donor**
You need to add hydrogen across the $C=O$ of the aldehyde to make a primary alcohol, $R-CHO \rightarrow R-CH_2OH$, but leave the $C=C$ alone. $NaBH_4$ does exactly this selective reduction, so it is the ideal reagent for reaction 1.
Final answer: $NaBH_4$ / sodium borohydride (or $LiAlH_4$ / lithium tetrahydridoaluminate).

hints: Look at Q and R and see that $H$ and $OH$ have added across the $C=C$ bond of T to give alcohols, so think of the hydration reaction of alkenes.
Recall the specific reagent and catalyst used industrially to add steam across a double bond.
walkthrough:
Recognise hydration of the alkene**
T to Q plus R is addition of $H-OH$ across the $(CH_3)_2C=CH-$ double bond. The aldehyde is untouched. This is the classic hydration reaction.

Recall the exact conditions**
Hydration uses steam, $H_2O(g)$, with concentrated phosphoric acid, $H_3PO_4$, as catalyst. That combination supplies $H^+$ to start electrophilic addition and then water to form the alcohol.

Final answer: Reagent: $H_2O(g)$ / steam.
Conditions: $H_3PO_4$ catalyst / phosphoric acid catalyst (high temperature and high pressure).

hints: Think about the first step of addition of $H^+$ to the $C=C$ bond and the two possible carbocation intermediates that can lead to Q and R.
Count how many alkyl groups are attached directly to the positive carbon in each possible intermediate.
Recall how alkyl groups stabilise a carbocation through electron donation and what this means for the relative amounts of Q and R.
walkthrough:
Picture the two competing carbocations**
When $H^+$ adds to $(CH_3)_2C=CH-$, it can add to either end. Adding $H^+$ to the $CH$ end puts $C^+$ on the $(CH_3)_2C$ end, giving a tertiary carbocation that leads to Q. Adding the other way gives a secondary carbocation that leads to R.

Compare stability by alkyl groups**
The tertiary $C^+$ leading to Q is surrounded by three alkyl groups, while the secondary $C^+$ leading to R has only two. Alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive centre.

Use the inductive effect to pick the major product**
This electron push is the positive inductive effect. More alkyl groups means more stabilisation, lower energy intermediate and faster formation. So the route to Q dominates and Q is formed in higher yield.

Final answer: Q has the higher yield.
The carbocation intermediate leading to Q is more stable as the $C^+$ is bonded to three alkyl groups / more alkyl groups.
Greater positive inductive effect from alkyl groups stabilises the intermediate, so this pathway is favoured.

hints: Recall the colour change for acidified $K_2Cr_2O_7$ when it acts as an oxidising agent and is itself reduced.
List the functional groups in Q (aldehyde plus tertiary alcohol) and in R (aldehyde plus secondary alcohol).
Decide which of these groups can be oxidised by heating with acidified dichromate and what that means for the observation in each tube.
walkthrough:
Remember the dichromate colour change**
Acidified $K_2Cr_2O_7$ is orange. When it oxidises another molecule it is reduced to $Cr^{3+}$, which is green. So any oxidation gives orange to green.

Check Q for oxidisable groups**
Q has $-CHO$ at one end and a tertiary alcohol $-C(OH)(CH_3)_2$ at the other. Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids, but tertiary alcohols resist oxidation because there is no H on the $C-OH$ carbon. The aldehyde alone is enough to turn the solution green.

Check R for oxidisable groups**
R has $-CHO$ plus a secondary alcohol $-CH(OH)-$. Both are oxidisable on heating: aldehyde to carboxylic acid and secondary alcohol to ketone. So R also gives orange to green, in fact two oxidations occur.

Final answer: Q: orange to green.
R: orange to green.
Both contain $-CHO$ / aldehyde which is oxidised (to carboxylic acid), and R also contains a secondary alcohol which is oxidised (to a ketone). Tertiary alcohol in Q is not oxidised.

hints: Focus on what happens to the $-OH$ group of the secondary alcohol in R when $PCl_5$ is added, while the aldehyde group stays unchanged.
Recall the two inorganic products always formed alongside the chloroalkane when an alcohol reacts with $PCl_5$.
walkthrough:
Swap OH for Cl in R**
$PCl_5$ converts alcohols to chloroalkanes. Only the $C-OH$ changes: $-CH(OH)-$ becomes $-CH(Cl)-$. The $-CHO$ end is untouched. The new organic molecule has formula $C_{10}H_{19}ClO$.

Balance with the inorganic side**
The $OH$ oxygen and the rest of the $PCl_5$ end up as phosphorus oxychloride, $POCl_3$, plus hydrogen chloride, $HCl$. So the full equation is $R-OH + PCl_5 \rightarrow R-Cl + POCl_3 + HCl$.

Final answer: $R-OH + PCl_5 \rightarrow R-Cl + HCl + POCl_3$
Organic product: $CH_3CH(CH_3)CH(Cl)CH_2CH_2CH(CH_3)CH_2CHO$ / $C_{10}H_{19}ClO$.
Inorganic products: $HCl + POCl_3$.

hints: Think about what $PCl_5$ does if any water is present in the sample and why that would spoil the test for the alcohol.
Write the equation for the vigorous reaction between $PCl_5$ and water that produces white fumes.
walkthrough:
See water as a competitor**
$PCl_5$ reacts violently with water as well as with alcohols. If Q and R are wet, some $PCl_5$ will be used up by water instead of by the $-OH$ group, giving misleading observations.

Show the hydrolysis equation**
With a little water: $$H_2O + PCl_5 \rightarrow POCl_3 + 2HCl$$ With excess water it goes all the way to phosphoric acid: $$4H_2O + PCl_5 \rightarrow H_3PO_4 + 5HCl$$ Drying avoids this side reaction.

Final answer: Water hydrolyses / reacts with $PCl_5$, so it must be removed to prevent a competing reaction.
$H_2O + PCl_5 \rightarrow POCl_3 + 2HCl$ OR $4H_2O + PCl_5 \rightarrow H_3PO_4 + 5HCl$.
